docs.title: Home
docs.text: This is a fork from the original OTFP code hosted in Cameron Abrams' GitHub repository but has significantly diverged from upstream and is independently maintained.

docs.title: On the fly parameterization
docs.text:
OTFP computes free-energy surfaces (FES) in MD simulations via temperature-acceleration.

It is written in C and uses SWIG to provide a Tcl interface to be used with NAMD via TclForces.

The user and developer documentation is built with MkDocs. When published, the site is available at https://alexispaz.github.io/otfp/. For local reading while editing this repository, run:

mkdocs serve

OTFP builds libraries and executables with Meson. The full build instructions, dependencies, debug builds, example test workflow, and MkDocs commands are in the User Guide build page. An example of a typical local build is:

meson setup build --prefix="$PWD/usr"; meson install -C build

docs.title: Citations
docs.text:
The OTFP method is explained in detail in the original publication:

  • Abrams and Vanden-Eijnden. "On-the-fly free energy parameterization via temperature accelerated molecular dynamics." Chem. Phys. Lett., 547 (2012) 114–119. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cplett.2012.07.064

The extension of OTFP in 2D is explained in:

  • Paz, Maragliano, and Abrams. "Effect of Intercalated Water on Potassium Ion Transport through Kv1.2 Channels Studied via On-the-Fly Free-Energy Parametrization." J. Chem. Theory Comput., 14(5) (2018) 2743–2750. https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jctc.8b00024

The combination of OTFP with Replica Exchanges is described in:

  • Paz, Vanden-Eijnden and Abrams. "Polymorphism at 129 dictates metastable conformations of the human prion protein N-terminal β-sheet." Chem. Science, 8(2) (2016) 1225–1232. https://doi.org/10.1039/c6sc03275c

Other publications with OTFP method are:

  • Alberini, Paz, Corradi, Abrams, Benfenati and Maragliano. "Molecular Dynamics Simulations of Ion Permeation in human NaV Channels." J. Chem. Theory Comput., 19(10) (2023) 2953–2972. https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jctc.2c00990

  • Paz and Abrams. "Free Energy and Hidden Barriers of the β-Sheet Structure of Prion Protein." J. Chem. Theory Comput., 11(10) (2015) 5024–5034. https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jctc.5b00576

  • Paz and Abrams. "Testing Convergence of Different Free-Energy Methods in a Simple Analytical System with Hidden Barriers." Computation, 6(2) (2018) 27. https://doi.org/10.3390/computation6020027

docs.title: Known issues
docs.text:
In SWIG documentation it is written:

"As a final complication, a major weakness of C++ is that it does not define any sort of standard for binary linking of libraries. This means that C++ code compiled by different compilers will not link together properly as libraries nor is the memory layout of classes and data structures implemented in any kind of portable manner. In a monolithic C++ program, this problem may be unnoticed. However, in Tcl, it is possible for different extension modules to be compiled with different C++ compilers. As long as these modules are self-contained, this probably won't matter. However, if these modules start sharing data, you will need to take steps to avoid segmentation faults and other erratic program behavior. If working with lots of software components, you might want to investigate using a more formal standard such as COM."

Thus, it is recommended to compile OTFP using the same compiler used to compile NAMD.

Another problem that can arise is a segmentation fault when the TCL script of NAMD input loads the compiled cfacv.so shared library. This might be related with differences in the linking of the tcl library in NAMD and in the cfacv.so library. To find which tcl library is using NAMD execute ldd ./namd2. Use that library to compile cfacv.so.

If the tcl library is not found by ldd, it is probably linked static. In that case nm ./namd2 | grep Tcl will show the common symbols defined in the tcl library (e.g. Tcl_AppendResult). This make difficult to known which tcl version was used to compile NAMD. If using the tcl library of the actual system gives segmentation fault, sometimes the issue disappears if the user compiles their own Tcl library from source and uses that one to compile cfacv.so.

docs.title: Additional tools to handle chapeau object files
docs.text:
Cropping or expanding the CV space, create croped.ch

./chapcrop cryo.ch 4 18.40076 4 18.40076

Attempt to add chapeau object files together.

./chapadd croped_*ch

If attempt fail, it might be needed to adjust the size of chapeau objects to have the same number of knots using chapcrop

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: This page documents the current architecture during refactoring. It is meant for readers who need to understand the code shape before changing it or embedding OTFP in another driver. The refactor branch does not need to preserve backward compatibility, but it should preserve scientific behavior unless a feature is explicitly removed.

docs.title: Current Layers
docs.text: Layer Files Responsibility NAMD callback calcforces.tcl Register NAMD groups, load coordinates, call C/Tcl update flow, return forces and energy. Tcl setup cfacv.tcl, cvs.tcl, restraints.tcl, chapeau.tcl, data.tcl Parse user variables, allocate C objects through SWIG, and prepare runtime state. SWIG API cfacv.i, cvs.i, cfacv_tcl.h, cvs_tcl.h Expose a deliberate Tcl-facing C API. Runtime public API cfacv.h Expose opaque runtime, restraint, and optimizer types plus user/SWIG-facing setup and update functions. Runtime internals cfacv_internal.h, cfacv.c Define DataSpace, restraint, optimizer structs, and expose runtime helpers for CV computation, energy, and reporting. DataSpace fields use explicit total/count/ownership names for core readability. Runtime force loop cfacv_force.c Orchestrate per-step force clearing, restraint values, restraint forces, CV boundary forces, FES/chapeau updates, and target evolution. Driver embedding facade otfp_engine.h, otfp_engine.c Provide a small C API for non-Tcl drivers such as GEMS. DataSpace ownership cfacv_dataspace.c Allocate/free DataSpace, register atom centers, CVs, restraints, and FES/chapeau objects through focused state owners. Restraints cfacv_restraint.c Restraint construction, restart state, energy functions, boundary functions, and TAMD/SMD/ADAM target evolution. CV public API cvs.h Expose the opaque cv type and user/SWIG-facing CV lifecycle, type, reference, and setup helpers. CV internals cvs_internal.h, cvs.c, measurements.c Define the concrete cv layout, CV descriptors, boundary functions, and value/gradient calculations. FES/chapeau public API chapeau.h Expose the opaque chapeau type and user/SWIG-facing lifecycle, output, and restart functions. FES/chapeau internals chapeau_internal.h, chapeau.c Define the concrete chapeau layout and internal module contracts for lifecycle, grid metadata, and size/grid comparisons. FES/chapeau grid utilities chapeau_grid.c Crop, sum, and symmetrize chapeau grid statistics. FES/chapeau accumulation chapeau_accumulate.c Accumulate 1D/2D force statistics into chapeau matrices and hit masks. FES/chapeau IO chapeau_io.c Manage binary output, restart state, lambda loading, and replica serialization. FES/chapeau solver chapeau_solver.c Build reduced band matrices and solve chapeau coefficients with LAPACK. FES/chapeau evaluation chapeau_eval.c Evaluate 1D/2D simplex interpolation, gradients, and peak-file loading. Tools catbinsp.c, simetrize.c, addchapeaus.c, cropchapeaus.c Offline manipulation of chapeau outputs/states.

docs.title: Driver Boundaries
docs.text:
NAMD is currently the only complete production driver in this repository, but it is not the engine model. The desired architecture is:

Boundary Responsibility Core engine Own DataSpace, CVs, restraints, FES/chapeau state, per-step force/energy calculation, and restart/output scheduling. NAMD/Tcl adapter Translate NAMD TclForces callbacks and user Tcl variables into core engine calls. Mock adapter Emulate enough of NAMD TclForces for fast regression tests. Future GEMS adapter Bind the otfp_engine C facade from Fortran with iso_c_binding, without going through Tcl or SWIG.

The GEMS integration plan is documented in GEMS integration. Refactors should keep moving NAMD/Tcl assumptions out of the core engine boundary.

docs.title: Current NAMD Runtime Flow
docs.text:
NAMD calcforces
  -> loadcoords p
  -> Tcl_UpdateDataSpace
     -> DataSpace_centerPosition copies driver positions into DataSpace
     -> DataSpace_centerForce exposes accumulated forces after the force loop
     -> DataSpace_ComputeCVs
        -> cv.calc for every CV
     -> DataSpace_RestrainingForces
        -> compute restraint values from CV linear combinations
        -> compute restraint energy/force
        -> accumulate center forces into DataSpace.R
        -> apply CV boundary forces
        -> accumulate and solve chapeau state when FES is enabled
        -> evolve TAMD/SMD/ADAM restraint targets
        -> save restart state
     -> addforce for each NAMD group
     -> addenergy from DataSpace_RestraintEnergy

docs.title: Public API Boundaries
docs.text:
The chapeau API has been split so SWIG sees only the opaque public interface:

  • chapeau.h declares typedef struct CHAPEAU chapeau plus public lifecycle, output, and restart functions.
  • chapeau_internal.h defines struct CHAPEAU and the internal module functions used by C modules and command-line tools.
  • Runtime orchestration uses chapeau helper functions for sampling, accumulation, solve scheduling, output scheduling, and default restart saves instead of writing chapeau fields directly.
  • cvs.h declares typedef struct cv cv plus public CV helpers.
  • cvs_internal.h defines struct cv, type lookup helpers, and the internal calculation/boundary functions used by the C runtime.
  • Runtime force orchestration uses CV helper functions for compute, value, gradient, boundary force, and output scheduling; direct CV field access is limited to CV implementation code.
  • cfacv.h declares opaque DataSpace, restraint, and optimizer types plus the supported C runtime setup/update API.
  • cfacv_internal.h defines the runtime structs and internal force/evolution helpers used by C modules. It also owns low-level constructors, type lookup helpers, debug dump helpers, and file wrappers that are not part of the public C or Tcl API.
  • Runtime force orchestration uses restraint helper functions for value accumulation, energy/force calculation, output scheduling, chapeau sampling, target evolution, and energy reads; direct restraint field access is limited to restraint implementation and restart serialization.

The SWIG surface no longer includes the broad C headers directly:

  • cfacv.i includes cfacv_tcl.h.
  • cvs.i includes cvs_tcl.h.

These Tcl headers declare only the functions used by the main Tcl setup/runtime flow: DataSpace lifecycle and setup, CV setup helpers, restraint setup and target updates, per-step compute/force/energy calls, and chapeau restart calls. They intentionally do not export lower-level constructors, type lookup helpers, debug dump helpers, or internal chapeau evaluation/serialization routines.

The remaining broad C headers are still used for C compilation and tests. During the next refactor passes, continue splitting them into:

  • Internal headers for C modules.
  • Tool-only headers if needed.
  • Narrow C headers for tests and external embedding, if that remains a supported use case.

This is the first step before deleting or renaming functions.

docs.title: Data Ownership
docs.text:
Current allocated objects:

  • DataSpace
  • atomCenterStruct
  • cv
  • restraint
  • tamdOptStruct
  • smdOptStruct
  • adamOptStruct
  • chapeau

The refactor branch now has destructors for the core runtime objects:

  • atomCenterStruct_free
  • centerStruct_free
  • cv_free
  • restraint_free
  • DataSpace_free
  • chapeau_free

The lifecycle Meson test exercises the basic constructor/destructor path for DataSpace, atom centers, one CV, and one restraint. Broader ownership tests should be added as modules are split.

docs.title: DataSpace Direction
docs.text:
DataSpace is the current legacy core context object. It is not a physical model object like a center, CV, restraint, or chapeau. It owns the runtime state that a driver needs for one OTFP calculation, and should be treated as a transitional container while the state is split into clearer objects.

Responsibility Current fields Centers centers, a CenterSet with atom-center definitions plus their _total and _count fields. CVs cvs, a CvSet with collective variables plus their total and count fields. Restraints restraints, a RestraintSet with restraints, checkpoint filename, and save frequency. Center step state center_step, a CenterStepState with center positions for driver input and center forces returned to the driver. FES state fes, a FesState with chapeaux and accumulate/solve scheduling. Restart/output Restraint restart policy lives in RestraintSet; chapeau output policy lives in each chapeau.

The target organization is to keep a single engine/context object but split its responsibilities into clearer subobjects:

  • center definitions;
  • CV definitions;
  • restraint state and restart policy;
  • step state for center positions, center forces, and bias energy;
  • FES state and solve/output scheduling;
  • restart/output policy tied to the state it persists.

The center buffers are owned by CenterStepState. Driver-facing code writes positions through DataSpace_centerPosition and reads forces through DataSpace_centerForce. Core force code updates the force buffer through DataSpace_clear_ctr_forces and DataSpace_add_ctr_force.

Center definitions are owned by CenterSet, CV definitions by CvSet, restraints by RestraintSet, and the FES state by FesState. Runtime modules use internal accessors such as DataSpace_cv, DataSpace_rstr, DataSpace_fes, and the count helpers. These accessors are a migration aid, not the target architecture: the target is to keep moving runtime behavior toward the objects with clearer names and responsibilities.

docs.title: High-Value Refactor Targets
docs.text: Target Problem Suggested direction cfacv.c Mixes construction, force loop, output, restart, target evolution, and OTFP solve orchestration. Split into dataspace, restraint, evolution, and force_loop modules. cvs.c Switch-heavy factory, global setup state for ZSD CVs, and all CV implementations in one file. Use CV descriptor tables and per-CV parameter structs. Internal state headers Chapeau, CV, and restraint state are isolated, and runtime orchestration now uses focused helper APIs for their hot paths and diagnostics. Tools, serialization, and implementation modules still access fields directly. Keep narrowing direct field access where it reduces coupling without obscuring numerical code. SWIG headers Internal helpers become Tcl-visible API. Expose a small deliberate API. Error handling Most failures call exit, which is hard to test and hard to recover from Tcl. Return status codes in C and convert to Tcl errors at the boundary. Allocation Constructors do not consistently initialize optional pointers; most types lack frees. Introduce zero-initializing constructors and destructors.

docs.title: Refactor Sequence
docs.text:
1. Narrow the Tcl/SWIG API to deliberate user-facing functions.
  2. Replace broad direct struct access with focused helper APIs where it reduces coupling.
  3. Expand the driver-oriented C embedding facade for GEMS and non-NAMD tests.
  4. Decide explicitly which experimental/legacy features remain.

docs.title: Behavior Guardrails
docs.text:
Fast tests should pass after each mechanical refactor:

meson compile -C build
meson install -C build
meson test -C build examples

Documentation should be updated in the same commit when a user-visible feature, configuration key, or developer boundary changes.

docs.title: Code Audit
docs.text: This project has a mixed C/Tcl/NAMD workflow, so unused-code detection should be treated as a candidate list rather than an automatic deletion list.

docs.title: Static candidates
docs.text:
Use:

scripts/audit-unused-c-symbols.sh

The script lists C functions with few references in src/. Symbols exported through SWIG, Tcl, headers, or command line tools may still be public API and need manual review before removal. Increase or reduce the threshold with:

MAX_REFS=3 scripts/audit-unused-c-symbols.sh

docs.title: Review policy
docs.text:
Classify each candidate as one of:

  • public-api: exported through SWIG, Tcl, headers, or user workflows.
  • tool-entry: used by a command-line executable or external script.
  • dead: no internal or documented external use.
  • defer: unclear usage, keep until covered by tests.

Only remove dead routines after the example regression suite passes.

docs.title: Areas to inspect first
docs.text:
• Collective variable variants in src/cvs.c.
  • Experimental or generated files under examples/, scripts/ana_tamd/, and lumo/.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
OTFP can be built with Meson. A typical local build installs into usr/ inside the repository:

meson setup build --prefix="$PWD/usr"
meson compile -C build
meson install -C build

The examples expect the installed Tcl scripts and shared libraries under that prefix.

The installed otfp_engine.h header is the supported C embedding facade for external drivers. The lower-level C headers are still internal refactor surfaces unless documented otherwise.

Use meson configure build after setup to inspect available project options. Use meson dist -C build when you need a source distribution.

docs.title: Documentation site
docs.text:
The documentation is built with MkDocs from the repository root:

mkdocs build

This writes the HTML site to site/. The directory is generated output and is ignored by git.

For local reading while editing:

mkdocs serve

Then open the URL printed by MkDocs, usually http://127.0.0.1:8000/.

For stricter checks before committing documentation changes:

mkdocs build --strict --site-dir /tmp/otfp-mkdocs-site

If MkDocs fails before building pages, check that mkdocs and the readthedocs theme are available in the active Python environment. The theme is part of a normal MkDocs installation, but minimal or isolated environments may need MkDocs installed explicitly.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
Required build tools and libraries:

  • C compiler.
  • Meson and Ninja.
  • MkDocs for documentation builds.
  • SWIG.
  • Tcl development package.
  • BLAS, LAPACK, and LAPACKE with pkg-config metadata.

The BLAS/LAPACK provider can be selected at setup time:

meson setup build --prefix="$PWD/usr" \
  -Dblas=blas \
  -Dlapack=lapack \
  -Dlapacke=lapacke

docs.title: Debug builds
docs.text:
For debugging with NAMD or the mock runner:

meson setup build --prefix="$PWD/usr" --buildtype=debug \
  -Dc_args='-g3 -O0 -fno-omit-frame-pointer' \
  -Dc_std=gnu11

For sanitizer builds:

meson setup build --prefix="$PWD/usr" --buildtype=debug \
  -Db_sanitize=address,undefined \
  -Dc_args='-g3 -O0 -fno-omit-frame-pointer' \
  -Dc_std=gnu11

When running NAMD with AddressSanitizer, the sanitizer runtime may need to be preloaded:

LD_PRELOAD="$(gcc -print-file-name=libasan.so)" namd3 +p1 job0.namd

For optimized local builds:

meson setup build --prefix="$PWD/usr" --buildtype=release \
  -Doptimization=3 \
  -Dwarning_level=0 -Dwerror=false \
  -Db_ndebug=true -Dstrip=true

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Examples live under examples/. The most useful regression examples are:

Example Description OTFP One-dimensional OTFP workflow. OTFP2D Two-dimensional OTFP workflow. OTFP2D_periodic Two-dimensional periodic collective variable workflow. adam Adaptive-moment style workflow. embedding Minimal C driver example using otfp_engine.h without Tcl/NAMD.

Most runnable examples use:

cd examples/OTFP
export CFACV_BASEDIR=../../usr
./run.sh

The regression runner uses src/mock.tcl, so it can exercise Tcl-level logic without a NAMD binary.

docs.title: C embedding example
docs.text:
The examples/embedding directory demonstrates the driver-facing API intended for GEMS and other non-NAMD programs. It includes only otfp_engine.h, links against libcfacv, computes one step, and prints the bias energy and center forces.

After installing locally:

cc examples/embedding/embedding.c \
  -Iusr/include -Lusr/lib -Wl,-rpath,"$PWD/usr/lib" -lcfacv \
  -o /tmp/otfp-embedding
/tmp/otfp-embedding

docs.title: Adding an example test
docs.text:
1. Keep the NAMD input in test mode by default.
  2. Generate compact deterministic outputs.
  3. Add reference files under examples/<name>/reference/.
  4. Register the output checks in examples/test.sh.
  5. Run meson test -C build examples after installing into usr/.

Use absolute tolerances only where numeric noise is expected; otherwise prefer exact comparisons.

docs.title: Extending OTFP
docs.text: This section is for developers or integration agents who need to change OTFP, embed it in another program, or continue the refactor.

docs.title: Current Direction
docs.text:
OTFP is being prepared as a vendored engine for GEMS while preserving the existing NAMD/Tcl workflow. New core code should avoid depending on Tcl, SWIG, or NAMD concepts. Those belong at adapter boundaries.

The preferred external C boundary is otfp_engine.h. Lower-level DataSpace_* functions are part of the historical C/Tcl API and should not be the default integration target for new drivers.

docs.title: What To Read
docs.text:
1. Architecture explains the current code layers, runtime objects, and ownership boundaries.
  2. GEMS integration explains how a Fortran driver should call the C facade.
  3. Testing lists the fast guardrails that should run after C refactors.
  4. Code audit records current simplification targets and known risks.

docs.title: Refactor Rules
docs.text:
• Preserve scientific behavior unless a feature is explicitly removed and documented.
  • Prefer mechanical splits before semantic rewrites.
  • Keep fast tests passing while moving code.
  • Update user and developer documentation in the same change as visible behavior, API, or architecture changes.
  • Keep the Tcl/SWIG adapter narrow. Do not expose internal helpers through Tcl unless the supported workflow requires them.

docs.title: AI-Assisted Development
docs.text:
This refactor branch may include code and documentation changes prepared with AI coding assistants under human direction. Treat AI output like any other contribution: review the diff, run the relevant fast tests, keep commits coherent, and make the scientific or architectural intent explicit in the commit message.

Do not rely on AI-generated text as a source for scientific claims, licensing claims, or citations. Those claims should remain traceable to the repository history, source publications, license files, or primary documentation.

docs.title: Good Extension Targets
docs.text:
• Add focused tests for geometry routines, chapeau restart/load paths, and repeated Fortran embedding steps.
  • Continue splitting chapeau code by lifecycle, IO, solver, evaluation, and accumulation responsibilities.
  • Keep moving core behavior behind clear objects: center definitions, CVs, restraints, step state, and FES/chapeau state.
  • Replace hard exits with status returns at the C boundary, then translate those failures into Tcl errors in the Tcl adapter.

docs.title: Features
docs.text: This page describes the functional surface that should be preserved or intentionally replaced during refactoring.

docs.title: NAMD/TclForce Integration
docs.text:
OTFP is loaded from a NAMD input script through:

tclforcesscript $CFACV_BASEDIR/include/calcforces.tcl
source $CFACV_BASEDIR/include/cfacv.tcl

Runtime flow:

  1. cfacv.tcl loads libcfacv.so and the Tcl helper files.
  2. parse_pdb reads labelPDB; atom occupancy stores mass and beta stores the 1-based center id.
  3. NewDataSpace allocates the C-side state.
  4. cvs_setup registers collective variables.
  5. rlist_setup registers restraints.
  6. chapeau_setup registers OTFP/FES state when FES(...) is defined.
  7. NAMD calls calcforces every step.
  8. Tcl_UpdateDataSpace copies group positions into C, computes CVs, computes restraint forces, copies forces back to NAMD groups, and adds restraint energy.

The test runner uses src/mock.tcl to simulate enough NAMD behavior for fast regression tests.

docs.title: Collective Variables
docs.text:
Configured with:

set cv(num) 1
set cv(1.type) BOND
set cv(1.centers) {1 2}

Supported C CV types:

Type Centers Notes BOND 2 Distance between two centers. HALFBOND 2 Distance with force only on the first center. BONDS even number Sum of pair distances. ANGLE 3 Angle over three centers. DIHED 4 Dihedral angle. S even number Bond-network switching CV. CARTESIAN_X 1 X coordinate of one center. CARTESIAN_Y 1 Y coordinate of one center. CARTESIAN_Z 1 Z coordinate of one center. COGX one or more Average x coordinate of centers. COGY one or more Average y coordinate of centers. COGZ one or more Average z coordinate of centers. LINE one or more Projection between two reference PDB states. RMSD one or more Mean squared displacement from a reference PDB. CHARMMD 4 CHARMM-style dihedral energy CV using n, k, and d. GAUSS2D 5 Two-dihedral Gaussian function. D2CHAP 5 Two-dihedral CV evaluated from a chapeau file. ZSDCIRCLE one or more Z-spread in a cylindrical selection. Uses global setup state. ZSDXRANGE one or more Z-spread in an x range. Uses global setup state. ZSDRING one or more Z-spread in a ring. Uses global setup state.

CV output:

set cv(1.outfile) "phi.x"
set cv(1.outfreq) 100

CV boundaries:

Boundary Behavior NADA No CV boundary force. SOFTUPPER Harmonic upper wall using max and boundk. SOFTLOWER Harmonic lower wall using min and boundk. SOFT Both soft walls using min, max, and boundk. AMD Adds the CV value as a local bias and applies unit force to the CV.

docs.title: Restraints
docs.text:
Configured with:

set restr(num) 1
set restr(1.cv) 1
set restr(1.k) 1500
set restr(1.type) tamd

A restraint is a linear combination of CVs. If restr(i.cvc) is omitted, equal weights are assigned across restr(i.cv).

Restraint potential functions:

Function Behavior HARMONIC Harmonic potential. HARMCUTO Harmonic potential with cutoff behavior.

Restraint boundary functions:

Boundary Behavior NADA No restraint boundary. SOFTUPPER Harmonic upper wall. SOFTLOWER Harmonic lower wall. SOFT Both soft walls. PBC Periodic wrapping over configured min/max. PERIODIC Periodic wrapping over [-pi, pi].

Restraint evolution types:

Type Required parameters Purpose TAMD g, dt, plus temp or biasf Brownian evolution of the restraint target. SMD target, ini, end Constant-velocity steering. ADAM a, b1, b2, e; optional tmin, decay Adaptive target evolution with termination.

Restraint output:

set restr(1.outfile) "phi.r"
set restr(1.outfreq) 100

docs.title: OTFP/FES Reconstruction
docs.text:
Configured by defining FES(...) before sourcing cfacv.tcl:

set FES(dm) 2
set FES(min) {-3.141592653589793 -3.141592653589793}
set FES(max) { 3.141592653589793  3.141592653589793}
set FES(knots) {151 151}
set FES(period) {1 1}
set FES(start) 0
set FES(solve.start) 0
set FES(solve.freq) 2500
set FES(outfile) job0
set FES(outfreq) 2500
set FES(outlvl) 3

Capabilities:

  • One-dimensional and two-dimensional chapeau grids.
  • Optional periodic grid dimensions.
  • Accumulation of force statistics from TAMD restraints.
  • Dense LAPACK solve path.
  • Binary output via *_chN.bsp.
  • Restart state via *.chN.
  • Lambda export through catbinsp.
  • Serialization helpers for replica-exchange communication.

docs.title: Restarts
docs.text:
Supported restart data:

  • Restraint targets through DataSpace_save_restraints and DataSpace_load_restraints.
  • Chapeau state through chapeau_savestate, chapeau_loadstate, and chapeau_loadlambda.
  • Example restart scripts set restart_otfp or restart_chapeau, then source the same workflow.

docs.title: Replica Workflows
docs.text:
The scripts under scripts/RE*.namd support NAMD replica workflows:

  • REMD_NVT.namd and REMD_NPT.namd: replica exchange molecular dynamics.
  • REOTFP_NVT.namd and REOTFP_NPT.namd: replica exchange with OTFP.
  • REOFP_NPT.namd: replica exchange using OTFP free-energy estimates.

Replica OTFP features include:

  • NUMREP chapeau objects.
  • Per-replica chid remapping on restraints.
  • Chapeau serialization and aggregation across replicas.
  • Restart script generation.

docs.title: Command-Line Tools
docs.text: Tool Purpose catbinsp Read binary chapeau output and print selected output levels. chapsim Symmetrize two-dimensional chapeau state. chapadd Add compatible chapeau states. chapcrop Crop or expand a chapeau grid.

docs.title: Fast Test Coverage
docs.text:
The fast regression suite currently covers mock-driven examples:

  • OTFP
  • OTFP2D
  • OTFP2D_periodic
  • CVs
  • adam

Run it through Meson:

meson test -C build examples

docs.title: GEMS Integration Plan
docs.text:
This page describes how to prepare OTFP for integration into GEMS as an in-tree free-energy engine.

The goal is not to preserve OTFP as a standalone community dependency. OTFP is stable laboratory code, while GEMS is the active experimentation environment for free-energy methods and non-NAMD potentials such as DFTB and tight-binding models. The practical integration path is to vendor the OTFP core into GEMS and drive it from GEMS, while keeping the NAMD/Tcl path as an adapter.

docs.title: Current Shape
docs.text:
OTFP currently has four conceptual parts:

Part Current files Role Core engine cfacv*.c, cvs*.c, chapeau*.c, public/internal headers Owns CVs, restraints, chapeau accumulation, solve scheduling, restart state, and force/energy calculation. NAMD adapter calcforces.tcl, cfacv.tcl, cvs.tcl, restraints.tcl, chapeau.tcl, data.tcl Converts NAMD TclForces data and user Tcl variables into core engine calls. Tcl/SWIG boundary cfacv.i, cvs.i, cfacv_tcl.h, cvs_tcl.h Exposes the selected C API to Tcl. This is an adapter boundary, not the engine model. Mock adapter mock.tcl, examples/test.sh, selected examples Emulates enough NAMD TclForces behavior to run fast regression tests without a full NAMD calculation.

For GEMS, the core engine is the useful part. The Tcl/SWIG and NAMD layers are reference adapters and regression tools.

docs.title: Engine Model
docs.text:
A molecular driver does not need to know about Tcl or NAMD. It needs a step-level OTFP engine with this lifecycle:

  1. Allocate one DataSpace.
  2. Register atom centers with masses and atom indices.
  3. Register CVs.
  4. Register restraints.
  5. Optionally register chapeau/FES state.
  6. On each step, copy current center positions into DataSpace.
  7. Compute CV values.
  8. Compute restraint forces, chapeau accumulation, target evolution, and restart/output scheduling.
  9. Read forces from DataSpace center buffers and add them to the driver.
  10. Read restraint energy and add it to the driver energy accounting.
  11. Free the DataSpace and owned objects at shutdown.

The current public C calls that match this model are:

Stage Current C API Allocate/free NewDataSpace, DataSpace_free Register centers DataSpace_AddAtomCenter Register CVs DataSpace_add_cv, set_zsd_circle, set_zsd_ring, set_d2chap, set_line, cv_access_ref, cv_access_ref2 Register restraints DataSpace_AddRestr, restr_AddTamdOpt, restr_AddSmdOpt, restr_AddAdamOpt Register FES DataSpace_SetupChapeau, DataSpace_get_chapeau Step update DataSpace_centerPosition, DataSpace_ComputeCVs, DataSpace_RestrainingForces Read results DataSpace_centerForce, DataSpace_RestraintEnergy, restr_getz, restr_getu Restart hooks DataSpace_save_restraints, DataSpace_load_restraints, chapeau_savestate, chapeau_loadstate, chapeau_loadlambda

This API is usable, but it still reflects the historical Tcl/NAMD workflow. New driver code should prefer the embedding facade in otfp_engine.h instead of teaching GEMS every historical function.

docs.title: Recommended GEMS Strategy
docs.text:
Use OTFP as vendored source inside GEMS, not as an external installed dependency:

  • GEMS is the active laboratory for the methods.
  • OTFP has limited standalone maintenance pressure.
  • Keeping the code in-tree makes it easier to couple OTFP with GEMS potentials, integrators, restart formats, and future free-energy experiments.
  • The NAMD adapter can remain as an optional compatibility path or regression reference.

Do not translate the whole OTFP codebase to Fortran before integration. The lower-risk path is:

  1. Keep the numerical core in C.
  2. Add a small C embedding facade with stable names and ownership rules.
  3. Bind that facade from Fortran using iso_c_binding.
  4. Translate or rewrite pieces later only when the integration shows a clear benefit.

This avoids mixing language conversion, build-system migration, memory ownership changes, and scientific validation in one step.

docs.title: Embedding Facade
docs.text:
The first driver-oriented facade lives in otfp_engine.h and otfp_engine.c. It is intentionally thin: it wraps DataSpace without changing numerical behavior. Its purpose is to give GEMS one stable dependency point while the Tcl/NAMD-facing internals continue to be refactored.

Meson installs otfp_engine.h next to the Tcl adapter scripts under the configured include directory. Consumers should include only this header for the embedding path.

See examples/embedding for a minimal C driver that uses this facade without Tcl, SWIG, NAMD, or the mock adapter.

Current API:

typedef struct otfp_engine otfp_engine;

otfp_engine *otfp_engine_create(int ncenters, int ncvs, int nrestr, long seed);
void otfp_engine_free(otfp_engine *engine);

int otfp_engine_add_center(otfp_engine *engine, int natoms,
                           const int *indices, const double *masses);
int otfp_engine_set_center_position(otfp_engine *engine, int center,
                                    const double xyz[3]);
const double *otfp_engine_center_force(otfp_engine *engine, int center);

int otfp_engine_add_cv(otfp_engine *engine, const char *type, int ncenters,
                       const int *centers, double zmin, double zmax,
                       const char *boundary, double boundary_k);
int otfp_engine_add_restraint(otfp_engine *engine, double k, double target,
                              int ncvs, const double *coefficients,
                              const char *function, double zmin, double zmax,
                              const char *boundary, double boundary_k);
int otfp_engine_add_tamd(otfp_engine *engine, int restraint,
                         double gamma, double kt, double dt,
                         int chapeau_id, int chapeau_dim);
int otfp_engine_add_smd(otfp_engine *engine, int restraint,
                        double target, int first_step, int last_step);
int otfp_engine_add_adam(otfp_engine *engine, int restraint,
                         double step_size, double beta1, double beta2,
                         double epsilon, double decay, double kt,
                         double min_step);

int otfp_engine_compute(otfp_engine *engine, int first_step, int step,
                        double external_bias);
double otfp_engine_bias_energy(otfp_engine *engine);

Ownership and data rules:

  • otfp_engine_create allocates the engine and owned OTFP state.
  • otfp_engine_free releases all owned state and accepts NULL.
  • Center, CV, and restraint setup arrays are copied by the underlying OTFP constructors; callers do not need to keep those temporary arrays alive after setup.
  • otfp_engine_add_restraint returns the zero-based restraint index, or -1 on failure. Use that index to attach TAMD, SMD, or ADAM evolution options.
  • otfp_engine_set_center_position writes the current position for one center.
  • otfp_engine_compute computes CVs, restraint forces, chapeau updates, target evolution, and bias energy for one step.
  • otfp_engine_center_force returns a pointer to the internal force buffer for one center after otfp_engine_compute; callers must copy it before the next position update or compute call.
  • Center and CV indices are C-style zero-based indices.

docs.title: Fortran Binding Notes
docs.text:
The first GEMS integration should use iso_c_binding against the embedding facade. The repository now includes tests/embedding_fortran.f90 as a minimal working example.

  • Store the opaque C handle as type(c_ptr).
  • Pass scalar integers as integer(c_int) or the exact width chosen by the C facade.
  • Pass coordinates and forces as contiguous real(c_double) arrays.
  • Keep allocation and destruction on the C side.
  • Convert Fortran strings to C strings only at setup time; avoid string-heavy calls in the per-step path.
  • Document index base rules explicitly. OTFP internals use C-style indices in the C API; Tcl scripts often translate from user-facing 1-based data.

The initial Fortran layer should be thin. Its job is to map GEMS data structures into the C facade and return forces/energies to GEMS. The smoke test constructs the same two-center BOND CV and harmonic/SMD restraint as the C embedding test, computes one step, reads a force pointer with c_f_pointer, and checks that force and energy values are finite.

docs.title: Work To Do Before Asking Another Agent To Integrate
docs.text:
1. Keep docs/architecture.md current with core/adapter boundaries.
  2. Extend the C embedding facade as GEMS needs more setup features.
  3. Expand the C embedding example toward GEMS-like repeated-step setup.
  4. Expand the Fortran iso_c_binding example toward the setup patterns GEMS will need.
  5. Expand the embedding tests beyond lifecycle/finite-value checks.
  6. Decide how OTFP will be vendored in GEMS: subtree under lib/, direct source import under a free-energy module, or a temporary development copy.
  7. Only after the C/Fortran boundary is working, evaluate whether any C modules should be rewritten in Fortran.

docs.title: What Not To Do Yet
docs.text:
• Do not make GEMS call the SWIG/Tcl API.
  • Do not require NAMD concepts in the engine-facing API.
  • Do not translate all CV/chapeau code to Fortran before integration.
  • Do not change numerical behavior while only moving adapter boundaries.

docs.title: Tcl Configuration Reference
docs.text:
OTFP's original user interface is a Tcl layer loaded from a NAMD input script. The Tcl files parse user variables, create the C-side objects through SWIG, and let calcforces.tcl exchange positions, forces, and energies with NAMD TclForces.

The usual entry point is:

tclforcesscript $CFACV_BASEDIR/include/calcforces.tcl
source $CFACV_BASEDIR/include/cfacv.tcl

CFACV_BASEDIR should point to the local install prefix, for example ../../usr from many example directories.

docs.title: Basic Tcl Shape
docs.text:
The Tcl setup uses global associative arrays. Keys follow the pattern name(index.field).

set cv(num) 1
set cv(1.type) BOND
set cv(1.centers) {1 2}

set restr(num) 1
set restr(1.cv) 1
set restr(1.k) 1500
set restr(1.type) tamd

This means: create one collective variable, define it as the distance between centers 1 and 2, then create one restraint acting on that CV.

docs.title: Centers
docs.text: Centers are weighted atom groups. In the NAMD workflow they are usually read from labelPDB: occupancy stores the atom mass and beta stores the 1-based center id. OTFP then registers those groups with NAMD and uses their center positions during the force callback.

docs.title: Collective Variables
docs.text:
Collective variables are configured through cv(...).

set cv(num) 1
set cv(1.type) BOND
set cv(1.centers) {1 2}
set cv(1.outfile) "distance.cv"
set cv(1.outfreq) 100

Common types include BOND, ANGLE, DIHED, Cartesian coordinates, RMSD, line projections, and chapeau-based CVs. The complete type list is in Feature reference.

docs.title: Restraints
docs.text:
Restraints are configured through restr(...).

set restr(num) 1
set restr(1.cv) 1
set restr(1.k) 1500
set restr(1.type) tamd
set restr(1.outfile) "distance.r"
set restr(1.outfreq) 100

A restraint can act on one CV or a linear combination of CVs. If restr(i.cvc) is omitted, OTFP assigns equal weights to the listed CVs.

The main evolution modes are:

Type Use TAMD Temperature-accelerated evolution of the restraint target. SMD Constant-velocity steering between initial and final targets. ADAM Adaptive target evolution.

docs.title: FES and Chapeau Settings
docs.text:
FES reconstruction is enabled by defining FES(...) before sourcing cfacv.tcl.

set FES(dm) 2
set FES(min) {-3.141592653589793 -3.141592653589793}
set FES(max) { 3.141592653589793  3.141592653589793}
set FES(knots) {151 151}
set FES(period) {1 1}
set FES(start) 0
set FES(solve.start) 0
set FES(solve.freq) 2500
set FES(outfile) job0
set FES(outfreq) 2500
set FES(outlvl) 3

The chapeau basis is the kernel used to accumulate force statistics on the FES grid. Changing the basis would affect which grid points receive accumulated statistics and may also affect the solve step.

docs.title: Restarts
docs.text: Example restart scripts usually set restart_otfp or restart_chapeau before sourcing the normal setup files. Restraint targets and chapeau state are loaded through the Tcl/SWIG layer, then the force callback continues from the restored state.

docs.title: Tcl References
docs.text:
Useful references when editing OTFP Tcl scripts:

  • Tcl language manual: https://www.tcl.tk/man/tcl8.6/TclCmd/contents.htm
  • NAMD TclForces documentation: https://www.ks.uiuc.edu/Research/namd/2.14/ug/node48.html
  • SWIG Tcl documentation: https://www.swig.org/Doc4.1/Tcl.html

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
The main regression entry point is:

examples/test.sh

After configuring and installing locally, it is also available through Meson:

meson setup build --prefix="$PWD/usr"
meson compile -C build
meson install -C build
meson test -C build examples

There is also a small C lifecycle test:

meson test -C build lifecycle

It constructs and frees a minimal DataSpace with atom centers, one CV, and one restraint. This test is intentionally narrow; it catches constructor, destructor, and link-level regressions before the slower example suite runs.

The C embedding facade has its own smoke test:

meson test -C build embedding

It constructs an otfp_engine, registers two centers, one BOND CV, and one harmonic restraint with SMD target evolution, then computes one step without sourcing Tcl or using the mock NAMD adapter. This is the first guardrail for future GEMS integration.

When a Fortran compiler is available, Meson also builds and runs an iso_c_binding smoke test:

meson test -C build embedding-fortran

This test exercises the same otfp_engine path from Fortran and verifies that opaque handles, C strings, contiguous arrays, and returned force pointers can be used from a Fortran caller.

The script runs from examples/ and checks selected output files against each example's reference/ directory.

docs.title: Current coverage
docs.text:
The current test set combines low-level lifecycle, C embedding, and optional Fortran embedding tests with high-level example behavior. The example runner is valuable because it exercises Tcl wrappers, the mock NAMD interface, chapeau output, and numeric regression files together.

Recommended next additions:

  • Small C unit tests for measurements.c geometry routines.
  • Chapeau serialization/load round-trip tests.
  • Error-path tests for missing or incompatible restart files.
  • More Fortran coverage for GEMS-like setup and repeated steps.
  • A CI job that builds, installs into usr/, and runs meson test.

docs.title: User Guide
docs.text: This section is for users who need to build OTFP, install it into a local prefix, and run the examples. It assumes basic command-line familiarity, but it does not assume that the reader has worked with NAMD TclForces or the OTFP C code before.

docs.title: What problem does OTFP solve?
docs.text:
Molecular dynamics gives atom positions and forces as a function of time. Many questions, however, are easier to ask in terms of a few collective variables (CVs), such as a distance, an angle, a dihedral, or a reaction coordinate. OTFP uses those CVs to estimate a free-energy surface while the simulation is running.

In practical terms, OTFP sits between a molecular dynamics driver and a biasing method:

  1. The driver provides the current positions of selected centers.
  2. OTFP computes CV values from those centers.
  3. Restraints apply bias forces on the CVs.
  4. OTFP converts those CV forces back into forces on the centers.
  5. When FES reconstruction is enabled, chapeau basis functions accumulate the statistics needed to reconstruct the free-energy surface.

docs.title: Vocabulary
docs.text: Term Meaning in this code Center A group of one or more atoms represented by a weighted position, usually a center of mass. CV A collective variable computed from one or more centers. Examples: distance, angle, dihedral. Restraint A bias potential applied to one CV or a linear combination of CVs. Target The restraint reference value. It can be fixed or evolved by TAMD, SMD, or ADAM. Chapeau The basis/kernel function used to accumulate free-energy statistics on a grid. FES Free-energy surface reconstructed from accumulated statistics.

docs.title: What should a new user run first?
docs.text:
Start by building and installing OTFP into usr/ inside the repository:

meson setup build --prefix="$PWD/usr"
meson compile -C build
meson install -C build

Then run the fast example suite:

meson test -C build examples

The examples use a mock Tcl/NAMD adapter, so they are useful for checking the OTFP setup quickly without launching a full NAMD calculation.

docs.title: Reading the examples
docs.text:
Most user-facing examples are Tcl scripts that configure centers, collective variables, restraints, and optional FES reconstruction before the driver starts the force loop. Read them in this order:

  1. docs/build.md for compiler, Meson, and installation steps.
  2. docs/examples.md for runnable examples and the mock regression workflow.
  3. docs/tcl-reference.md for the Tcl variables used by OTFP.
  4. docs/features.md for the complete list of supported CVs, restraints, chapeau/FES settings, restarts, and tools.

The NAMD/Tcl workflow follows these conceptual steps:

  1. Define centers.
  2. Define CVs from those centers.
  3. Define restraints on the CVs.
  4. Optionally define chapeau/FES settings.
  5. For each simulation step, copy center positions into OTFP.
  6. Ask OTFP to compute CVs, bias forces, target evolution, and FES updates.
  7. Copy the returned center forces back into the driver.

To see the driver-facing API without Tcl or NAMD, run the C embedding example:

cc examples/embedding/embedding.c \
  -Iusr/include -Lusr/lib -Wl,-rpath,"$PWD/usr/lib" -lcfacv \
  -o /tmp/otfp-embedding
/tmp/otfp-embedding

That example is the closest starting point for understanding how another code, such as GEMS, should call OTFP.
